title: Practical integration and system evaluation
overview: Evaluate a health information system as connected information work: clarify its purpose and users, map workflow and data, assess system fit, identify controls, and defend a recommendation with evidence and trade-offs. The Map → Select → Control → Defend framework organizes this process, while HIM responsibilities protect information quality, meaning, trust, and use.
objectives: Connect purpose, users, workflow, data, systems, controls, and measures in a practical recommendation.
Evaluate a health information system across functional, information, governance, and adoption fit.
Use the Map → Select → Control → Defend framework to explain system integration and defend a recommendation with evidence and trade-offs.
Explain HIM responsibilities for protecting information quality, meaning, trust, and use.

sections.body: A system evaluation is more than a feature list. A practical recommendation connects the system's purpose to its users, workflow, data, systems, controls, and measures. Begin by identifying what work the system is meant to support, who uses it, what information moves through it, and which decisions depend on that information. Then consider whether the system fits the work and whether its controls and measures protect the intended outcome. A strong recommendation states its rationale concisely and acknowledges one trade-off and a mitigation.
sections.title: Evaluate the system as connected information work

sections.body: A workflow map represents people, systems, data, decisions, and control points. Mapping these elements makes it possible to explain what happens, who is responsible, and where control is needed. For example, a community hospital can trace registration, clinical documentation, laboratory, patient portal, coding, billing, quality reporting, and follow-up as one information flow. Treating these activities as connected work helps frame system fit and responsibilities across the flow, rather than judging an isolated screen or task.
sections.title: Map the information flow before selecting systems

sections.body: Use four distinct questions when evaluating an information system. Functional fit asks whether it supports the actual work. Information fit asks whether data are complete, meaningful, exchangeable, and retrievable. Governance fit asks whether privacy, security, and accountability are addressed. Adoption fit asks whether people can use, learn, and sustain the system. These dimensions are complementary: support for work does not by itself establish that information can be understood or exchanged, and governance protections do not by themselves establish that people can use the system and sustain its use.
sections.title: Assess four dimensions of system fit

sections.body: The Map → Select → Control → Defend framework provides a practical sequence. Map people, process, data, and decisions. Select systems that support the workflow. Add quality, privacy, security, and audit controls. Defend the recommendation with evidence and trade-offs. Evidence can include requirements, decision criteria, data-quality checks, and implementation risks. A defensible recommendation uses these considerations to explain its rationale, makes a trade-off visible, and identifies a mitigation rather than presenting the choice as cost-free.
sections.title: Use evidence to defend a recommendation

sections.body: HIM professionals connect system purpose to trustworthy information work. They explain purpose by identifying users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits. They protect meaning through definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation. They protect quality by checking identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency. They support trust through privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure. They also help improve workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction. These responsibilities connect system evaluation to safe, useful, and accountable information work.
